text_blocks.snippet: A rash caused by kidney problems can present in different ways, but often appears as small, dome-shaped, itchy bumps that may join together to form larger, rough, and raised patches. It can also include blisters, and may be accompanied by dry, cracked skin and changes in skin color.
snippet_highlighted_words: small, dome-shaped, itchy bumps that may join together to form larger, rough, and raised patches

list.snippet: Bumps: The most common manifestation is small, dome-shaped bumps that are extremely itchy.
Raised Patches: These bumps can merge to form larger, rough, and raised patches.
Blisters: In some cases, blisters may develop, particularly in end-stage kidney disease.
Dryness and Cracking: The skin may become very dry, tight, and prone to cracking.
Itching: Intense itching, known as uremic pruritus, is a common symptom.
Color Changes: Skin may appear pale or have a yellowish tint, and nails can also be affected.
Calcium Deposits: Calcium deposits can form under the skin, causing bumps or lesions.
Location: Rashes can occur anywhere on the body, but are often found on the face, back, and the arm with the dialysis fistula.

text_blocks.snippet: If you experience these symptoms, especially if accompanied by other signs of kidney disease, it's crucial to consult with a doctor for proper diagnosis and treatment.

text_blocks.snippet: A body rash can stem from various causes, including skin conditions, allergic reactions, infections, and even systemic diseases. Common causes include contact dermatitis, eczema, psoriasis, and various infections. Understanding the specific type of rash and its associated symptoms is crucial for proper diagnosis and treatment.
snippet_highlighted_words: skin conditions, allergic reactions, infections, and even systemic diseases

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at some common causes:

list.title: Contact Dermatitis:
list.snippet: This rash results from direct contact with an irritant or allergen, like poison ivy, nickel, or certain chemicals.

list.title: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis):
list.snippet: A chronic condition often linked to allergies and asthma, causing itchy, red, and scaly patches.

list.title: Psoriasis:
list.snippet: A condition where skin cells build up too quickly, leading to red, scaly patches, often on joints and the scalp.

list.title: Seborrheic Dermatitis:
list.snippet: A condition causing redness and scaling, especially around the eyebrows, nose, and scalp (often called dandruff or cradle cap in infants).

list.title: Heat Rash:
list.snippet: Caused by blocked sweat ducts, leading to small, itchy bumps, especially in hot and humid weather.
Bacterial Infections: Staph infections can occur through cuts, leading to sores and potentially spreading.
Viral Infections: Chickenpox, shingles, and other viral infections can cause rashes.
Fungal Infections: Ringworm and athlete's foot are fungal infections that cause itchy, circular rashes.
Parasitic Infections: Lice and other parasites can also cause skin irritation and rashes.
Food Allergies: Certain foods can trigger rashes in susceptible individuals.
Medication Allergies: Some medications can cause skin reactions.
Insect Bites and Stings: Reactions to insect bites and stings can cause localized redness, swelling, and itching.
Systemic Diseases: Lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and other autoimmune diseases can manifest with skin rashes.
Certain Medications: Some medications can have skin rashes as a side effect.
If the rash is severe, widespread, or accompanied by other symptoms like fever, breathing difficulties, or swelling.
If the rash is painful, oozing, or doesn't improve with home care.
If you suspect a serious infection or allergic reaction.
